summary: Recommends that active queue management be tested, standardized and widely deployed in network devices to improve Internet performance. It also urges continued research into better algorithms. It is a best current practice that updates earlier guidance.

plainLanguage.summary: When a network queue stays full, packets wait longer and some are discarded. This Best Current Practice recommends that network devices signal congestion before their queues fill, while allowing different algorithms to be chosen for different conditions.

questions: why is red no longer the default aqm
subtitle: Recommendations for keeping queues short and signaling congestion before buffers fill.

tldr.problem: Tail-drop queues signal congestion only when full, which creates delay, drops bursts of packets and can let some flows monopolize queue space.
tldr.mechanism: Network devices should use Active Queue Management (AQM) to mark or drop packets before queues fill. AQM should support ECN and should not require routine manual tuning or depend on a specific transport.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7567 replaces RFC 2309 and no longer recommends RED or another algorithm as the default. It also calls for research on flows that do not respond adequately to congestion signals.

today: RFC 7567 is a Best Current Practice published in July 2015. It obsoletes RFC 2309; the unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Queue Management Matters
sections.content:
Congestion can severely reduce service when routers and other network devices do not manage packet forwarding carefully. TCP congestion control helps endpoints reduce their sending rates, but the RFC says endpoint mechanisms alone are not sufficient in every condition.

Queue buildup is also a major source of latency. RFC 2309 introduced Active Queue Management (AQM) and recommended Random Early Detection (RED) by default. Experience showed that choosing RED parameters was difficult, so this RFC continues to recommend AQM without recommending a default algorithm.

The guidance applies to best-effort traffic and adaptive real-time traffic. AQM may be used in routers, switches, other middleboxes and endpoint networking stacks.
sections.plainLanguage: Full queues add delay and can reduce network performance. Network devices can help by signaling congestion before their buffers fill.

sections.title: Problems with Tail Drop
sections.content:
Tail drop accepts packets until a queue reaches its limit, then discards each new arrival until the queue drains. This can keep queues full for long periods, so packets wait and bursts from one flow may produce several losses.

The RFC identifies four drawbacks: persistent full queues, lock-out where one or a few flows take most queue space, bursts that delay other packets, and synchronization when flows sharing a bottleneck react to congestion at the same time. Random drop on full or head drop on full can address lock-out but do not solve persistent full queues.

AQM addresses the full-queue problem for responsive flows by marking or dropping packets before the buffer overflows. It can reduce delay and unnecessary loss, but it does not by itself provide general fairness among flows.
sections.plainLanguage: Tail drop waits until a queue is full before signaling congestion. AQM signals earlier so responsive senders can slow down before the buffer overflows.

sections.title: Queue Management, Scheduling and ECN
sections.content:
Queue management controls queue length by marking or dropping packets. Scheduling chooses which packet to send next and can allocate bandwidth among flows. The RFC treats them as complementary: scheduling alone does not control the size of each queue or the total queue.

Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) lets a device mark an ECN-capable packet instead of dropping it under suitable congestion. The receiver reports the mark to the sender, which can react before packet loss occurs. Devices still need to drop excessive traffic if a sender, receiver or network device fails to handle ECN correctly.

Buffer capacity is a separate choice from AQM thresholds. The buffer should generally hold the largest normal burst expected. AQM can keep the average queue short without requiring designers to reduce buffer capacity to an unsuitable level.
sections.plainLanguage: Scheduling chooses which packet goes next; AQM decides when to signal congestion. ECN can carry that signal as a mark, but devices must still limit traffic if endpoints ignore it.

sections.title: Flows That Ignore Congestion
sections.content:
The RFC distinguishes TCP-friendly flows, non-responsive flows and flows that respond less than TCP. A non-responsive flow does not reduce its rate after congestion signals. Less-responsive flows may reduce their rates, but less than a conformant TCP flow would under comparable conditions.

UDP itself does not provide congestion control. Some voice, video and bulk-data applications use UDP, and an application can even increase traffic in response to packet loss. Tunnels or many simultaneous short connections can also aggregate into traffic that responds less than a single TCP flow.

The RFC says there was no consensus solution for controlling congestion caused by these flows and limited measurement evidence about the scale of the threat. It calls for research into detection, mitigation and the appropriate definition of a flow.
sections.plainLanguage: Some traffic responds slowly or not at all when a network signals congestion. The RFC says more research is needed to manage these flows without harming other traffic.

sections.title: The Seven Recommendations
sections.content:
The RFC summarizes its guidance in seven recommendations, expressed with SHOULD because some unanticipated cases may differ. It recommends that network devices implement AQM to manage queue length, reduce latency and avoid lock-out. Deployed AQM algorithms should support ECN as well as packet loss.

Algorithms should not require routine operational tuning, should respond to measured congestion rather than application profiles, and should not interpret specific transport behavior. Congestion-control algorithms should use available capacity without undue loss or round-trip delay.

The final recommendation calls for research, engineering and measurement on flows that do not respond to congestion notification or behave more aggressively than current TCP.
sections.plainLanguage: The recommendations favor AQM that adjusts without routine manual tuning and works across transport types. They also call for continued work on traffic that does not respond to congestion.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
AQM can operate without inspecting application or transport details, which the RFC describes as privacy-enhancing. AQM and scheduling may reduce the ability of unresponsive traffic to take capacity from other flows.

Some denial-of-service traffic may be difficult to distinguish from legitimate traffic, such as tunnels carrying aggregated flows. The RFC therefore says that research should consider ways to reduce this risk. It states that the document itself introduces no new privacy issues.
sections.plainLanguage: AQM does not need to inspect application data, which limits the information a device needs to see. Unresponsive traffic can still disrupt other flows, and the RFC calls for further research on that problem.

items.label: Use AQM
items.desc: Manage queue lengths, reduce latency and avoid lock-out.

items.label: Support ECN
items.desc: Signal congestion with ECN as well as loss.

items.label: Avoid routine tuning
items.desc: Common use should not require operational parameter tuning.

items.label: Measure congestion
items.desc: Respond to measured congestion, not application profiles.

items.label: Transport independent
items.desc: Do not depend on specific transport behavior.

items.label: Use capacity
items.desc: Use available capacity without undue loss or round-trip delay.

items.label: Continue research
items.desc: Study flows that are unresponsive or more aggressive than TCP.
